chunks: Abu Ali Al-Ash'ari, from Muhammad ibn Abd al-Jabbar, from al-Hajjal, from Tha'laba, from Ma'mar ibn Amr, from Ata', from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:
The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'He did not lie to the reconciler.'
O caravan! Indeed, you are thieves.
Then he said: 'By Allah, they did not steal, and he did not lie.'
But the chief of them has done this, so ask them, if they can speak.
Then he said: 'By Allah, they had not done it, and he did not lie.'

key_terms.الْعِيرُ: The caravan (referring to the group in the story of Joseph)
key_terms.سَارِقُونَ: Thieves (the accusation made in the Quranic narrative)
key_terms.لَا كَذَبَ: Did not lie (indicating exemption from being called a liar in this context)
key_terms.مُصْلِحٍ: Reconciler (one who settles disputes between parties)

ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic ruling on lying for the sake of reconciliation?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi establishes the principle of 'al-kidhb li-l-islah' (lying for the sake of reconciliation), where the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him and his family) validates strategic omission or slight exaggeration to restore peace. He illustrates this by citing the narrative of Prophet Joseph (Yusuf), where the brothers' accusation of theft was a calculated ruse rather than a literal falsehood, thereby distinguishing between deceptive intent and purposeful narrative for harmony. This concept is central to Shia jurisprudence for determining when a statement that appears false is actually permissible or even praiseworthy.
